claude.sample_unit: head CT radiology reports (one per patient)

links.outcome: Accuracy comparison of three LLMs across three prompt strategies on same reports
links.effect: Claude significantly higher accuracy than GPT and Gemini for intracranial hemorrhage (p<0.0001); Gemini significantly lower than Claude and GPT for skull fracture (p<0.0001); Claude accuracy 0.98-0.99.
links.quote: In many comparisons, Claude demonstrated significantly higher accuracy than both GPT and Gemini ( p < 0.0001), while no statistically significant difference was observed between GPT and Gemini.

links.outcome: Effect of prompting strategy and repeated-run reproducibility on classification accuracy
links.effect: Claude and GPT stable across prompts; Gemini significantly higher with Chain of Thought than Standard or Self Consistency. Each combination run three times; reproducibility compared across runs.
links.quote: For both intracranial hemorrhage and skull fracture classification, Claude and GPT maintained relatively consistent accuracy across different prompting methods, whereas Gemini achieved significantly higher accuracy with Chain of Thought prompting than with either Standard or Self Consistency prompting.

links.outcome: Performance stratified by institution across three sites
links.effect: Stratified analysis by institution performed (details in supplement); institution-specific error patterns analyzed; prevalence varied by site (ICH 5.8%-46.2%). Site-level numbers not in main text.
links.quote: In addition, a stratified analysis by institution was performed.

links.outcome: Error analysis of LLM misclassifications of hemorrhage/fracture in reports
links.effect: Errors from ambiguous phrases, unchanged/old findings, post-surgical changes, and unrelated findings; e.g., 63 false negatives despite clear hemorrhage description, 69 false positives from 'cannot be identified'.
links.quote: Ambiguous phrases (e.g., “possible”) were associated with errors in both classification tasks.

unlisted_practices: Comparing prompting strategies (standard, chain of thought, self-consistency) for LLM structuring of radiology reports

links.outcome: candidate LLM accuracy for report structuring
links.effect: Claude hemorrhage accuracy was 0.98–0.99 versus GPT 0.97 and Gemini 0.97; Claude outperformed GPT/Gemini for hemorrhage and Gemini for skull fractures (p < 0.0001).
links.quote: Claude demonstrated significantly higher accuracy for intracranial hemorrhage than GPT and Gemini, and also outperformed Gemini for skull fractures (p < 0.0001).

links.effect: Accuracies were 0.97–0.99, but errors included 63 hemorrhage false negatives despite clear description and 69 false positives from “cannot be identified”; fracture errors included 21 post-craniotomy false positives.
links.quote: Error analysis revealed common challenges including ambiguous phrases and findings unrelated to intracranial hemorrhage or skull fractures, underscoring the importance of careful prompt design.

links.effect: Gemini Chain of Thought significantly outperformed Standard and Self Consistency for both labels (p < 0.0001); skull fracture accuracy 0.99 versus 0.98 and 0.98.
links.quote: For both intracranial hemorrhage and skull fracture classification, Claude and GPT maintained relatively consistent accuracy across different prompting methods, whereas Gemini achieved significantly higher accuracy with Chain of Thought prompting than with either Standard or Self Consistency prompting.

screen.practice: prompting strategy (chain of thought, self-consistency prompting)
screen.reason: Evaluated the performance impact of different prompt engineering strategies (Standard, Chain of Thought, Self Consistency) across three proprietary LLMs for extracting findings from free-text radiology reports.
